subjects.name: Albert Einstein
clues: As a young man he worked as a clerk in a Swiss patent office, checking inventions.
In his 'miracle year' of 1905 he published four groundbreaking scientific papers.
He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the photoelectric effect.
He left Germany in 1933 and spent his later years in Princeton, New Jersey.
The wild-haired scientist behind the theory of relativity and the equation E = mc².
subjects.fact: In 1952 he was offered the presidency of Israel, and politely turned it down.

subjects.name: Isaac Newton
clues: Late in life he ran England's Royal Mint and chased down coin forgers.
He built the first practical reflecting telescope, using a mirror instead of lenses.
He developed calculus, which led to a bitter quarrel with Gottfried Leibniz.
His 1687 book, the Principia, set out three famous laws of motion.
A falling apple is said to have inspired his law of universal gravitation.

links.name: Albert Einstein
links.rel: had his ideas on gravity extended by

subjects.fact: He was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705.

subjects.name: Galileo Galilei
clues: Born in Pisa in 1564, he started out studying medicine before switching to maths.
He studied swinging pendulums and how objects speed up as they fall.
In 1610 he discovered four large moons circling Jupiter.
In 1633 he was put on trial for teaching that the Earth moves around the Sun.
The Italian scientist, often called the father of modern science, who improved the telescope.
subjects.fact: He was born in the same year as William Shakespeare.

subjects.name: Stephen Hawking
clues: He was born on 8 January 1942, exactly 300 years after Galileo died.
He held the Lucasian chair of mathematics at Cambridge, once held by Isaac Newton.
He predicted that black holes should slowly leak a faint glow of radiation.
His 1988 book A Brief History of Time became a worldwide bestseller.
This British physicist used a wheelchair and spoke through a computer voice because of motor neurone disease.

links.name: Isaac Newton
links.rel: held the same Cambridge chair as

links.name: Galileo Galilei
links.rel: was born 300 years to the day after the death of

subjects.fact: He appeared as himself in The Simpsons and in Star Trek: The Next Generation.

subjects.name: Niels Bohr
clues: He played in goal at football; his brother Harald won an Olympic silver medal for Denmark.
He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922.
In 1913 he described electrons circling the nucleus in fixed energy levels.
He had famous friendly debates with Albert Einstein about quantum theory.
This Danish physicist gave his name to a famous model of the atom.
subjects.fact: Element 107, bohrium, is named after him.

subjects.name: Richard Feynman
clues: As a boy in New York he repaired neighbours' radios for fun.
He shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on how light and matter interact.
He invented simple drawings that show how particles interact, now named after him.
At the Challenger disaster inquiry he dipped an O-ring in ice water to show how cold made it fail.
The bongo-playing American physicist whose memoir is called 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. ...!'

links.name: Albert Einstein
links.rel: once gave a seminar attended by

subjects.fact: He liked to crack safes and open locked filing cabinets as pranks on his colleagues.

subjects.name: Michael Faraday
clues: He had little schooling and taught himself science as a bookbinder's apprentice.
He began as an assistant to the chemist Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution in London.
In 1825 he started the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people.
In 1831 he discovered how a moving magnet can create an electric current.
A metal cage that blocks electric fields is named after this English scientist.
subjects.fact: The farad, the unit of electrical capacitance, is named after him.

subjects.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
clues: He was a church official who also practised medicine and wrote about money.
He was born in 1473 in the city of Toruń.
His great book on the heavens was published in 1543, the year he died.
His big idea pushed the Earth out of the centre of the universe.
The Polish astronomer who said that the Earth and planets orbit the Sun.
subjects.fact: Legend says he was handed a printed copy of his book on the day he died.

subjects.name: Johannes Kepler
clues: He served as imperial mathematician to the Holy Roman Emperor in Prague.
He worked as assistant to the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe.
He discovered that planets travel in ovals called ellipses, not perfect circles.
His three laws of planetary motion were later explained by Isaac Newton.
A NASA space telescope that hunted for planets around other stars was named after this German astronomer.
subjects.fact: He also wrote Somnium, an early science-fiction story about a journey to the Moon.

subjects.name: Edwin Hubble
clues: Before turning to astronomy, he studied law at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar.
He worked at Mount Wilson Observatory in California with its giant 100-inch telescope.
In the 1920s he showed that the Andromeda 'nebula' is a separate galaxy far beyond ours.
He found that distant galaxies are moving away from us, so the universe is expanding.
A famous space telescope launched in 1990 is named after this American astronomer.
subjects.fact: He was born in Missouri in 1889.

subjects.name: Carl Sagan
clues: He won a Pulitzer Prize in 1978 for his book The Dragons of Eden.
He helped put together the golden records carried by the two Voyager spacecraft.
He named a famous photo of Earth seen from far out in space the 'Pale Blue Dot'.
His novel Contact became a 1997 film starring Jodie Foster.
The American astronomer who presented the 1980 TV series Cosmos.

links.name: Voyager 1
links.rel: helped send a golden record aboard

subjects.fact: An asteroid, 2709 Sagan, is named in his honour.

subjects.name: Marie Curie
clues: Born in Warsaw, she studied at a secret 'Flying University' because women could not enrol.
She moved to Paris to study and married a fellow scientist, Pierre.
She discovered two new elements, naming one of them after her homeland.
She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and the first person to win one in two sciences.
The Polish-French pioneer of radioactivity who discovered radium.
subjects.fact: Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes.

subjects.name: Dmitri Mendeleev
clues: He was born in Siberia, the youngest child of a very large family.
He taught chemistry at the university in Saint Petersburg.
In 1869 he arranged all the known elements by weight in rows and columns.
He left gaps for undiscovered elements and correctly predicted what they would be like.
The Russian chemist who created the periodic table.
subjects.fact: Element 101, mendelevium, is named after him.

subjects.name: Antoine Lavoisier
clues: He also worked as a tax collector, a job that cost him his life in the French Revolution.
His wife, Marie-Anne, helped with his experiments and drew his equipment.
He gave oxygen and hydrogen their names.
He showed that in a chemical reaction, mass is neither created nor destroyed.
This Frenchman is known as the father of modern chemistry.
subjects.fact: He also served on the commission that helped create the metric system.

subjects.name: Rosalind Franklin
clues: During her career she studied the structure of coal, viruses and DNA.
She was an expert in X-ray crystallography at King's College London.
An X-ray picture from her lab, known as Photo 51, revealed DNA's twisted shape.
Watson and Crick used her data to build their double helix model in 1953.
A European Mars rover was named after this British scientist, who died in 1958.
subjects.fact: She died at 37, four years before the Nobel Prize for the DNA structure was awarded.

subjects.name: Alfred Nobel
clues: He spoke several languages and also wrote poetry and a play.
Late in life he owned Bofors, a Swedish steel and weapons maker.
In 1867 he patented an explosive that made blasting rock much safer.
A famous story says a newspaper printed his obituary by mistake, calling him a 'merchant of death'.
His will paid for famous yearly prizes in peace, literature and the sciences.
subjects.fact: Element 102, nobelium, is named after him.

subjects.name: Charles Darwin
clues: He was born on the very same day as Abraham Lincoln: 12 February 1809.
He began training as a doctor in Edinburgh but could not bear watching surgery.
He spent five years sailing around the world aboard HMS Beagle.
Finches and giant tortoises of the Galápagos Islands helped shape his thinking.
His 1859 book On the Origin of Species explained evolution by natural selection.
subjects.fact: His face appeared on the Bank of England £10 note from 2000 to 2018.

subjects.name: Gregor Mendel
clues: He was a monk, and later the abbot, at a monastery in Brno.
He grew thousands of pea plants in the monastery garden.
He tracked traits like flower colour and seed shape across generations.
His work was ignored for decades until scientists rediscovered it around 1900.
This friar is known as the father of genetics.

links.name: Charles Darwin
links.rel: lived at the same time as

subjects.fact: He also kept bees and recorded the weather.

subjects.name: Louis Pasteur
clues: He was born in 1822 in Dole, France, the son of a tanner.
He helped save the French silk industry from a disease killing silkworms.
In 1885 he gave a rabies vaccine to a boy who had been bitten by a dog.
He proved that germs cause disease and that life does not appear from nothing.
Heating milk to kill harmful germs is named after this French scientist.
subjects.fact: The research institute he founded in Paris opened in 1888.

subjects.name: Jane Goodall
clues: As a small child in England she was given a toy chimpanzee called Jubilee.
In 1960 she went to Tanzania to study wild animals, without a university degree.
She saw apes stripping twigs to fish termites out of mounds: animals making tools.
She gave the apes she studied names, like David Greybeard, instead of numbers.
The British scientist famous for decades of studying wild chimpanzees at Gombe.
subjects.fact: She founded her research and conservation institute in 1977.

subjects.name: Carl Linnaeus
clues: He was a botanist and doctor who taught at Uppsala University.
He sent students on voyages around the world to collect plants.
He sorted living things into groups such as classes, orders, genera and species.
He gave humans the scientific name Homo sapiens.
This Swede created the two-part Latin naming system used for every species.
subjects.fact: He gave scientific names to thousands of plants and animals.

subjects.name: Hippocrates
clues: He was born around 460 BCE on the Greek island of Kos.
He taught that illnesses have natural causes, not punishments from the gods.
Writings linked to him say health depends on a balance of four body 'humours'.
New doctors often still recite a promise, the oath named after him.
The ancient Greek physician known as the father of medicine.
subjects.fact: A plane tree on Kos is said to grow where he taught his students.

subjects.name: Ibn Sina
clues: Born near Bukhara around 980, he was treating patients while still a teenager.
He is said to have learned the whole Quran by heart by the age of ten.
He wrote on philosophy, astronomy and music as well as medicine.
His medical encyclopedia was a standard textbook in European universities for centuries.
The great Persian doctor of the Islamic Golden Age who wrote The Canon of Medicine.
subjects.fact: His tomb is in the city of Hamadan in Iran.

subjects.name: Alexander Fleming
clues: Born on a Scottish farm, he worked in army hospitals in France during World War I.
In the early 1920s he found lysozyme, a germ-fighter in tears.
In 1928 he noticed that mould had killed the bacteria on a dish left out during a holiday.
He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.
The Scottish doctor who discovered penicillin.
subjects.fact: His messy lab at St Mary's Hospital in London is now a small museum.

subjects.name: Edward Jenner
clues: He was a country doctor in Gloucestershire, England.
He showed that baby cuckoos push other eggs out of their nests.
He noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed safe from smallpox.
In 1796 he tested his idea on James Phipps, an eight-year-old boy.
He created the world's first vaccine, against smallpox.

links.name: Louis Pasteur
links.rel: was honoured in the word 'vaccine' by

subjects.fact: The word vaccine comes from the Latin 'vacca', meaning cow.

subjects.name: Sigmund Freud
clues: Trained as a nerve doctor, he worked in Vienna for most of his life.
In 1938 he moved to London, where his last home is now a museum.
He believed dreams reveal hidden wishes and wrote The Interpretation of Dreams.
He popularised the 'talking cure', with patients lying on a couch.
The Austrian founder of psychoanalysis.
subjects.fact: His famous couch is on display at the Freud Museum in London.

subjects.name: Thomas Edison
clues: He was mostly taught at home and became partly deaf at a young age.
As a young man he worked as a telegraph operator.
His lab at Menlo Park, New Jersey, was called an 'invention factory'.
In 1877 he invented the phonograph, which could record and play back sound.
The American inventor with over 1,000 patents who made a long-lasting electric light bulb.
subjects.fact: The company General Electric grew out of his businesses.

subjects.name: Nikola Tesla
clues: He was born in 1856 to a Serbian family in what is now Croatia.
He moved to New York in 1884 and briefly worked for Thomas Edison.
He developed the alternating current (AC) system that powers homes today.
His famous coil can throw giant, crackling sparks of electricity.
An electric car company founded in 2003 is named after this inventor.
subjects.fact: The unit of magnetic field strength is named after him.

subjects.name: Alexander Graham Bell
clues: His mother and his wife were both deaf, and he spent years teaching deaf students.
Born in Edinburgh, he moved to Canada and then to the United States.
He served as the second president of the National Geographic Society.
In 1876 he was granted a patent for a device that sends the human voice along a wire.
His first call was: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
subjects.fact: He suggested people answer calls by saying 'Ahoy!'

subjects.name: James Watt
clues: He worked as a scientific instrument maker at the University of Glasgow.
While repairing a model engine, he thought of adding a separate condenser.
He went into business with Matthew Boulton, building engines in Birmingham.
He came up with the word 'horsepower' to compare engines with horses.
A unit of power, printed on light bulbs, is named after this Scottish engineer.
subjects.fact: He appears with Matthew Boulton on the Bank of England £50 note issued in 2011.

subjects.name: Johannes Gutenberg
clues: He was a goldsmith from the city of Mainz.
He invented a hand mould for casting metal letters quickly.
He also made an oil-based ink that would stick to metal type.
His famous Bible was printed around 1455.
The German who brought printing with movable type to Europe around 1440.
subjects.fact: Fewer than 50 copies of his Bible are known to survive.

subjects.name: Wright Brothers
clues: Before taking to the skies, this pair ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio.
They tested gliders at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, for its steady winds.
They built their own wind tunnel to test the shapes of wings.
On 17 December 1903 their Flyer made the first powered, controlled flight.
The two American siblings who invented the first successful airplane.
subjects.fact: The first flight in 1903 lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres.

subjects.name: Guglielmo Marconi
clues: Born in Bologna, he did his first experiments in the attic of his family's house.
He moved to England, where he patented his invention in 1896.
In 1901 he sent the letter S in Morse code across the Atlantic Ocean.
He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The Italian inventor who pioneered long-distance radio.
subjects.fact: When he died in 1937, many radio stations fell silent for two minutes in his honour.

subjects.name: Charles Babbage
clues: He waged a long campaign against noisy street musicians in London.
He held the Lucasian chair of mathematics at Cambridge.
He designed the Difference Engine to calculate number tables without mistakes.
His planned Analytical Engine had a memory store and a 'mill', like a modern computer.
The English mathematician called the 'father of the computer', who worked with Ada Lovelace.
subjects.fact: In 1991 London's Science Museum built his Difference Engine No. 2, and it worked.

subjects.name: Pythagoras
clues: Born on the Greek island of Samos, he founded a community in southern Italy.
His followers lived by strict rules and reportedly refused to eat beans.
He linked music to numbers, finding that pleasing notes come from simple ratios.
He taught that, deep down, everything in the universe is made of numbers.
A famous rule about right-angled triangles, a² + b² = c², is named after him.
subjects.fact: Hundreds of different proofs of his triangle theorem are known.

subjects.name: Euclid
clues: Almost nothing is known about his life, except that he taught in Alexandria.
He is said to have told a king that there is 'no royal road' to geometry.
He proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
His book, the Elements, was used to teach geometry for over 2,000 years.
The ancient Greek mathematician known as the father of geometry.
subjects.fact: The Elements is one of the most widely printed books in history.

subjects.name: Archimedes
clues: He lived in the Greek city of Syracuse on the island of Sicily.
He worked out the value of pi more accurately than anyone before him.
He designed war machines, including a giant claw said to lift enemy ships.
Of levers he said: 'Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.'
He is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath after a big discovery.
subjects.fact: A water-lifting device, a screw turned inside a tube, is named after him.

subjects.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
clues: As a schoolboy he reportedly added up all the numbers from 1 to 100 in moments.
As a teenager he showed how to draw a regular 17-sided shape with ruler and compass.
In 1801 he worked out the orbit of the lost dwarf planet Ceres so it could be found again.
He ran the observatory at Göttingen for nearly 50 years.
Called the 'Prince of Mathematicians', this German gave his name to the bell curve.
subjects.fact: He asked for a 17-sided shape on his gravestone; the stonemason refused, saying it would look like a circle.

subjects.name: Fibonacci
clues: As a boy he travelled with his merchant father to North Africa.
There he learned the Hindu-Arabic numerals from local teachers.
His 1202 book Liber Abaci helped bring the digits 0 to 9 to Europe.
He posed a puzzle about how fast a pair of rabbits would multiply.
A number sequence named after him goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21...

links.name: Al-Khwarizmi
links.rel: helped spread the numerals described by

subjects.fact: His sequence turns up in nature, in the spirals of sunflower seeds and pine cones.

subjects.name: Al-Khwarizmi
clues: He was a scholar at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad.
He drew up star tables and worked on a map of the known world.
His book on Hindu numerals helped spread the decimal system to the West.
The word 'algebra' comes from the title of his book on solving equations.
The word 'algorithm' comes from the Latin form of his name.

links.name: Fibonacci
links.rel: had his numerals spread in Europe by

subjects.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
clues: Mostly self-taught, he worked as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust.
In 1913 he wrote to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, sending pages of new formulas.
In 1918 he became one of the youngest Fellows of the Royal Society.
The 'taxicab number' 1729 comes from a story about Hardy visiting him in hospital.
The Indian maths genius whose life is told in the film The Man Who Knew Infinity.
subjects.fact: India celebrates National Mathematics Day on his birthday, 22 December.

subjects.name: Aryabhata
clues: He wrote his main work in verse in 499 CE, when he was just 23.
He is linked with Kusumapura, near the city now called Patna.
He gave the value of pi as about 3.1416.
He taught that the Earth spins on its axis, causing day and night.
India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after this ancient mathematician.
subjects.fact: He correctly explained that eclipses are caused by shadows, not by demons.

subjects.name: Ada Lovelace
clues: Her father was the famous poet Lord Byron, whom she never really knew.
Her mother pushed her to study mathematics and logic from an early age.
She described her way of thinking as 'poetical science'.
In 1843 she published notes on Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine.
Her method for that machine is often called the first computer program.
subjects.fact: A day celebrating women in science is named after her and held every October.

subjects.name: Alan Turing
clues: He was a gifted long-distance runner who ran a marathon in under 2 hours 47 minutes.
In 1936 he described an imaginary machine that could carry out any calculation.
At Bletchley Park he helped crack the German Enigma code in World War II.
He suggested a test of whether a machine can think like a human.
The British codebreaker who appears on the Bank of England £50 note.
subjects.fact: The top prize in computer science, the Turing Award, is named after him.

subjects.name: Tim Berners-Lee
clues: Both of his parents worked on one of the first commercial computers.
He studied physics at Oxford and built a computer from an old television.
In 1989 at CERN he proposed a system for sharing documents through links.
He made the first website and the first web browser.
The British scientist who invented the World Wide Web.
subjects.fact: He chose not to patent his invention, so anyone could use it for free.

subjects.name: Grace Hopper
clues: As a girl she took apart alarm clocks to see how they worked.
She joined the US Navy Reserve in World War II and rose to rear admiral.
She was one of the first programmers of the Harvard Mark I computer.
Her team taped a moth found inside a computer into their logbook as the first real 'bug'.
This pioneer built an early compiler and helped create the COBOL programming language.
subjects.fact: A US Navy destroyer, USS Hopper, is named after her.

subjects.name: Socrates
clues: He served as a soldier and was known for walking about barefoot.
He never wrote anything down; we know him from his students' writings.
He taught by asking question after question, a method now named after him.
In 399 BCE an Athens jury sentenced him to death by drinking hemlock.
The Greek thinker who said he knew only that he knew nothing; teacher of Plato.
subjects.fact: He was famous for saying that the unexamined life is not worth living.

subjects.name: Plato
clues: He wrote in dialogues, often with his teacher as the main speaker.
He told a story of prisoners in a cave who see only shadows on a wall.
He wrote about Atlantis, a mighty island said to have sunk into the sea.
He founded the Academy in Athens, an early school of higher learning.
Author of The Republic, he was the student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle.
subjects.fact: The word 'academy' comes from his school, named after the grove where it met.

subjects.name: Aristotle
clues: Born in Stagira in northern Greece, he was the son of a royal doctor.
He dissected and described hundreds of kinds of animals.
He founded a school called the Lyceum in Athens.
He spent about 20 years studying at Plato's Academy.
This Greek philosopher was the tutor of the young Alexander the Great.
subjects.fact: His school's members were nicknamed 'walkers' because they discussed ideas while strolling.

subjects.name: Confucius
clues: He was born in 551 BCE in the small state of Lu.
He spent years travelling between kingdoms, hoping a ruler would follow his advice.
He taught respect for parents and elders, good manners and honest government.
His students collected his sayings in a book called the Analects.
The Chinese teacher who said: 'Do not do to others what you would not want done to you.'
subjects.fact: His birthday is celebrated as Teachers' Day in Taiwan.

subjects.name: René Descartes
clues: He liked to stay in bed late in the morning to think.
He spent about twenty years of his working life in the Dutch Republic.
He invented the x and y coordinate system used to draw graphs.
He died in Stockholm after going to teach Queen Christina of Sweden.
The French philosopher who wrote 'I think, therefore I am'.
subjects.fact: A town in France where he was born is now named after him.

subjects.name: Immanuel Kant
clues: He spent almost his whole life in Königsberg, now Kaliningrad.
Neighbours supposedly set their clocks by his regular afternoon walk.
He suggested that the Sun and planets formed from a spinning cloud of gas.
His 1781 book Critique of Pure Reason is a landmark of philosophy.
The German philosopher known for the 'categorical imperative'.

links.rel: was born in a city now part of

subjects.fact: Besides philosophy, he lectured on geography for decades.
